phonemes.desc: Short open [ɐ]; the palatal nasal ñ follows, as in 'canyon'
Palatal nasal plus [dʑu] — mañju, 'gentle, sweet, lovely'
Palatal [ɕ] plus long close [iː] — śrī, 'glory, splendor'

pronunciation.approximation: mun-joo-SHREE — the ñ is the nasal of 'canyon'; śrī is one syllable, the 'sh' softened.
pronunciation.note: Mañjuśrī is a compound: mañju, 'gentle, sweet, lovely,' + śrī, 'glory, splendor' (Monier-Williams) — 'the Gentle Glory.' His other names are a litany of the same music: Mañjughoṣa, 'Gentle Voice'; Vāgīśvara, 'Lord of Speech.' The restoration keeps the palatal ñ, the ś, and the long ī; the ASCII 'Manjushri' loses all three. Tier-1 by rule: three distinctive letters preserved.

domains.title: The Gentle Glory
domains.subtitle: The Flaming Sword, the Book on the Lotus, and the Mountain of Five Terraces
domains.lead: Mañjuśrī is the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom: the ever-youthful prince who raises the flaming sword that cuts ignorance and bears the book of the Perfection of Wisdom on a blue lotus — the mind of every Buddha made visible as a sixteen-year-old with a blade.

cards.name: The Flaming Sword
cards.desc: The khadga that does not wound but severs: ignorance cut at the root, wisdom flaming at the edge.

cards.name: The Book on the Lotus
cards.desc: The Prajñāpāramitā volume resting on a blue utpala — the text the sword serves.

cards.name: The Lion Mount
cards.desc: He rides the lion of the teaching — wisdom's roar that no argument withstands.

cards.name: A Ra Pa Tsa Na
cards.desc: Oṃ A Ra Pa Tsa Na Dhīḥ — the Arapacana syllabary as mantra, recited across the Himalaya for a sharp mind.

symbols.name: The flaming sword
symbols.meaning: Discrimination that liberates: the cut that ends confusion, not the one that starts it

symbols.name: The blue lotus and the book
symbols.meaning: Wisdom as a text to be carried and a flower that opens by itself

symbols.name: The seed syllable Dhīḥ
symbols.meaning: The sound of insight itself, traced on children's tongues in the Himalaya

symbols.name: The lion mount
symbols.meaning: The vehicle of the teaching: majesty that roars once and settles every dispute

symbols.name: The sixteen-year-old form
symbols.meaning: Wisdom is not the slow deposit of years but the freshness of a mind that has not agreed to be confused

mythology.lead: Mañjuśrī's mythology is the biography of wisdom itself: he appears wherever the sūtras need the hardest question asked — and answered without a flicker. He debates laymen and nāga girls, drains lakes with a sword-stroke, teaches from a mountain that became China's greatest pilgrimage, and sends pilgrims out to find the truth for themselves.

myths.title: The Debate of Non-Duality
myths.text: When the layman Vimalakīrti feigned illness to draw the Buddha's disciples into dialogue, every bodhisattva found an excuse not to visit — each remembered being corrected by him once. Mañjuśrī alone went, leading the whole assembly, and their exchange crowns the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa (ch. 9, 'Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality'). Thirty bodhisattvas define non-duality by dissolving paired opposites — motion and rest, self and being, bondage and release — each more subtly than the last. Mañjuśrī declares that all their words are themselves dualistic, and that he has nothing to say. Vimalakīrti answers with silence, and Mañjuśrī pronounces the silence itself the teaching: 'Good sirs, this is truly the entrance into non-duality.' It is the most famous consultation in Buddhist literature — the wisdom bodhisattva certifying that the highest truth declines to be phrased.

myths.title: The Nāga King's Daughter
myths.text: In the twelfth chapter of Kumārajīva's Lotus Sūtra — the Devadatta chapter — Mañjuśrī returns from the nāga palace beneath the sea, where he had preached the Lotus, and reports that the dragon king's daughter, eight years old, has already attained the highest awakening. The elder Śāriputra objects on every ground his age could supply: a female body, a child, an animal's realm — surely the bodhisattva path cannot be completed so fast, in such a vessel. The girl appears, offers a precious jewel to the Buddha, and completes the path before the whole assembly; the sūtra lets her achievement answer the objection rather than argue it. Mañjuśrī's role is the chapter's quiet engine — he carries the teaching where it was never expected to go, into a palace under the sea. The myth is his brief for the universality of awakening: wisdom, taught well, does not check credentials.

myths.title: The Sword That Drained the Lake
myths.text: Nepal's own scripture, the Svayambhū Purāṇa, makes him the valley's founder. In the beginning the whole Kathmandu basin lay under a serpent lake, and at its center floated the self-existent flame — the svayambhū, the primordial light that needs no maker. Mañjuśrī came from the five-peaked mountain of China in the north, saw the flame resting on the waters, and resolved that beings must have a valley in which to venerate it. With one stroke of his sword he cut the gorge at Chobhar in the southern rim, and the lake drained away through the cleft, leaving a habitable plain; the flame remained on its hill, crowned today by the Svayambhū stūpa, its painted eyes watching over the city. The gorge and the stūpa still stand. It is his iconography read as geography: the sword that opens a way for beings to live and to worship.

myths.title: Clear-and-Cool Mountain
myths.text: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra names his earthly dwelling: a mountain in the northeast called Clear-and-Cool (Qīngliáng shān), where he teaches amid ten thousand bodhisattvas — 'in this mountain,' the sūtra says, dwells the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī with his assembly. Chinese Buddhists identified the peak with Wǔtái shān, the five-terraced mountain of Shanxi, and made it East Asia's greatest bodhisattva pilgrimage. Emperors climbed its terraces — the Tang and Qing courts endowed its temples lavishly — and Tibetan lamas and Mongol khans came seeking Wenshu's apparitions; the mountain's luminous cloud-halos, still photographed today, were read as the bodhisattva's own radiance, and sudden appearances of a rider on a lion became its standing miracle. Pilgrims still climb the terraces hoping for the lion. The myth means that wisdom is not only a doctrine to study but a place to go — and that the place, for fifteen centuries, has answered back.

myths.title: The Boy and His Fifty-Three Teachers
myths.text: The final chapter of the Avataṃsaka, the Gaṇḍavyūha, begins with a boy. Sudhana, the son of a merchant, is moved by the Buddha's teaching and seeks instruction; Mañjuśrī — his first teacher — sends him south with the words that set the whole pilgrimage walking: pursue the practice of a bodhisattva, and do not begrudge your life or comfort. Sudhana visits fifty-three (in the Chinese count) teachers in turn — monks, physicians, kings, shipwrights, an apothecary, a courtesan, a child, Maitreya in his tower of visions — and each sends him onward, until the last door opens back onto Mañjuśrī, who returns him into the world he left. The structure is the teaching: wisdom is a route, not a destination, and its path runs through every kind of life before arriving where it began.

lore.syncretism: He is the most portable of the great bodhisattvas: Wénshū in China, Monju in Japan, 'Jam dpal in Tibet. In Tibet his cult became inseparable from scholarship itself — Tsongkhapa venerated as his emanation, and the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, 'Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī,' recited as the daily liturgy of the monasteries (Wayman's translation made the text a classic in the West). With Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi he forms the lords of the three families — wisdom, compassion, and power — the triad painted over a thousand Himalayan doorways. His sword-and-book traveled the sea routes as well: his images stand in the temples of Buddhist Java. And in China the identification ran both ways — Wenshu was held to appear to worthy students as a humble stranger, testing them with a question before vanishing.
lore.culturalLegacy: Mañjuśrī is the patron saint of students across half the world: Himalayan children still have the syllable Dhīḥ traced on their tongues for a quick mind, and his Arapacana mantra is murmured before examinations from Ladakh to Lhasa. His iconography — sword in the right hand, book on the lotus at the left — is the universal Buddhist shorthand for the two halves of wisdom, cutting and knowing. Mount Wutai, his earthly seat, is a UNESCO landscape where a dozen languages still call on Wénshū. In Japan, Monju presides over the school-examination season, his name invoked in June by students at temples from Tokyo to Kamakura. The restoration Mañjuśrī keeps the palatals and the long vowel of a name that, in every language it entered, never stopped meaning a sharp and gentle mind.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Mañjuśrī is the proof that clarity is a form of compassion: the sword is raised not against persons but against the fog that makes persons suffer. His youth is the point — wisdom is not the slow deposit of years but the freshness of a mind that has not agreed to be confused, and his sword is not a weapon but a diagnosis: confusion cut at the root, before it flowers into cruelty or despair.

He asks of every learner the one question his book and blade pose together: what are you willing to have cut, so that what remains can finally be read? The pairing is exact. A sword without a book is mere aggression; a book without a sword is mere storage. Mañjuśrī holds both, and the tradition holds him — at the head of every classroom, on every tongue that recites Dhīḥ — as the reminder that the gentlest sound and the sharpest cut are one motion when the mind is clear.

lore.archaeology: His mountain is the monument: Wǔtái shān preserves the Nanchan temple hall (782 CE) and the Foguang temple's East Hall (857 CE) — the two oldest surviving timber buildings in China — on the terraces pilgrims have climbed for fifteen centuries. The Kathmandu valley keeps his founding stroke in stone and water: the Chobhar gorge through which the lake drained, and the Svayambhū stūpa on its hill. His certain images emerge in the early centuries CE and multiply along the Silk Road; by the Pāla period the sword-and-book type was fixed, and it has not changed since. In Japan, Monju's seat at the temple Tōdai-ji — where the great Vairocana was dedicated in 752 — marks how closely wisdom bodhisattva and cosmic Buddha were paired in the Nara mind.
